claims.text: Applying a thin silicide coating to boride-based components will improve their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
The corrosion improvement will result from formation of a protective, self-healing oxide scale at plating temperatures.
Uncoated boride-based components are inherently vulnerable to attack by molten aluminum.
Pack cementation can be used to apply a silicide coating.
Pack cementation produces a thin silicide layer on the component surface.
Approximately 650–700 °C represents typical hot-dip aluminum-plating exposure conditions.
Oxygen must be present during molten-aluminum exposure to support formation of the protective oxide scale.
The coating process forms a surface silicide phase such as MSi2.
The surface silicide converts to a dense, SiO2-rich protective layer when exposed to oxygen.
The resulting SiO2 barrier is continuous and self-healing.
The SiO2 barrier impedes aluminum diffusion.
The SiO2 barrier prevents molten aluminum from readily wetting and attacking the boride substrate.
Silicide-coated boride components will have at least a one-order-of-magnitude lower corrosion rate than uncoated boride components in molten-aluminum plating baths.
The improvement will persist only while the coating remains continuous and mechanically intact.
The improvement will persist only below the stability limit of the silicide/oxide system and when sufficient oxygen is available.
Mechanical damage or extreme thermal conditions may compromise the coating's integrity.
Prior evidence on silicide-coated refractory high-entropy alloys indicates improved oxidation resistance.
Prior evidence on silicide-coated high-entropy alloys demonstrates dramatic reductions in oxidation rate.
The quantitative improvement for boride-based materials in molten aluminum remains uncertain and requires direct testing.
